title: Detection of Server
summary: This detection strategy covers the acquisition of server infrastructure, where an adversary rents or builds the systems that will host command and control, staging and payload delivery. It matters because every later stage of an operation depends on that infrastructure, and because rented servers are bought with payment and identity traces that do not belong to your network. The telemetry that makes it possible is cloud provider audit logs for compute and virtual machine creation, resource tagging events, DNS query logs for provider update hostnames, and procurement records for infrastructure purchases. It fails in practice because legitimate engineering teams create cloud instances constantly, so a rule based only on the creation event produces constant noise unless it is scoped by region, account, naming style and first seen behaviour.

beginner.definition: Server acquisition means an attacker gets a server to use during an attack. They may rent it from a cloud provider or buy it from a hosting company. This detection looks for the signs of that rental and of the first use of the new server.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker needs somewhere to send stolen data and to control infected machines. That place is a server they control. The purchase leaves a trail in provider logs and payment systems. Seeing the trail early can reveal an operation before it reaches your network. It also helps your incident team understand who is behind an event.
howItWorks: Cloud and hosting providers write an audit record when a new server is created, started or associated with an address.
Those records reach your SIEM only if you collect them, so the first step is to turn on that collection for every account you own.
The rule looks for new compute resources in regions or accounts where your teams have never built anything.
It adds context such as the identity that made the request, the naming pattern of the resource and whether the account has a change ticket.
Related signals from your own network, such as hosts resolving provider update names they never used before, are joined to the same case.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse sign in sheet. Regular staff sign in with the same names and the same shifts. A delivery van that arrives at two in the morning, parks in the wrong bay and asks for the back door is worth a second look, even if the paperwork is correct. The odd detail, not the arrival itself, is the signal.
takeaways: Server acquisition is a preparation step, so its traces live in provider logs, not on your endpoints.
The strongest signals are first use, unusual region and a mismatch with your normal naming style.
You must collect provider audit logs before this detection can work at all.

objectives: Explain why attackers need their own servers and where those servers are rented
Identify which provider audit events record the creation of new compute infrastructure
Establish a baseline of approved regions, instance types and naming patterns per account
Write a rule that flags new compute resources outside the approved pattern
Describe how provider evidence supports attribution and takedown requests
dataSources: AWS CloudTrail management events for RunInstances, RequestSpotInstances and AllocateAddress calls
Azure activity log entries for virtual machine creation and public IP address association
Google Cloud audit logs for compute instance insert operations with project and region fields
DNS resolver or passive DNS query logs showing first resolution of provider update hostnames from your network
logic: The pattern is the creation of server resources in a provider account outside the regions, sizes and naming conventions your organisation normally uses, especially when the requesting identity is a human user rather than an automation role and no matching change record exists. The fields to correlate are the account or project identifier, the region, the resource name and tags, the requesting principal and the creation time. The benign case is an automation role creating instances with your standard naming and tags in an approved region, while the malicious case shows a first seen principal, a new region, free form naming and immediate association of a public address.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Compute instance created outside approved regions and naming pattern
# logsource:
#   product: aws
#   service: cloudtrail
# detection:
#   selection:
#     eventName:
#       - RunInstances
#       - RequestSpotInstances
#     errorCode: absent
#   filter:
#     userIdentity.arn|contains: 'role/terraform'
#     awsRegion|in: approved_regions
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: medium
falsePositives: A disaster recovery exercise that builds temporary instances in a secondary region
A new engineering team that has not yet adopted the standard resource naming and tagging policy
Developer sandbox accounts where short lived instances are normal daily work
A training workshop or lab environment built once in a region your teams rarely use
tuningNotes: Build the approved region, size and tag list from ninety days of provider history before you enable the rule, then suppress automation roles by name and scope the rule to production accounts first. Keep first seen principal detection at full strength, because a human identity creating compute for the first time is rare and interesting. You lose visibility of infrastructure rented by an attacker outside your own accounts, which is the common case, so pair this rule with brand and domain monitoring rather than treating it as complete coverage.
